summary: capacitor 1 (C1) (Capacitor values) is what the Crossover calculator works out, and it gets there from the woofer impedance, the midrange impedance, the tweeter impedance and the crossover frequency. It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Crossover calculator work?
sections.html:
The Crossover calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports capacitor 1 (C1) (Capacitor values) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (number of speakers, the filter order type and the filter order type 3 way); then you type in the woofer impedance, the midrange impedance, the tweeter impedance and the crossover frequency.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Crossover calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Capacitor 1 (c 1)=(number of speakers, filter order type, tweeter impedance, crossover frequency)
Capacitor 1 (c 1)=(number of speakers, filter order type 3 way, spread, tweeter impedance, high crossover frequency)
Capacitor 2 (c 2)=(number of speakers, filter order type, woofer impedance, crossover frequency)
Capacitor 2 (c 2)=(number of speakers, filter order type 3 way, spread, midrange impedance, mid-range crossover frequency)
Capacitor 2 (c 2)=(number of speakers, filter order type, tweeter impedance, crossover frequency)
Capacitor 2 (c 2)=(number of speakers, filter order type 3 way, spread, tweeter impedance, high crossover frequency)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Frequency, opening in hertz
  • Frequency, opening in hertz
  • Frequency, opening in hertz
  • Inductance – henry, opening in millihenries
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Crossover calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the woofer impedance, the midrange impedance and the tweeter impedance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Crossover calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns capacitor 1 (C1) (Capacitor values), derived from the woofer impedance, the midrange impedance and the tweeter impedance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Crossover calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the woofer impedance, the midrange impedance, the tweeter impedance and the crossover frequency, which is 14 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter woofer impedance in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Woofer impedance opens in ohms and the chip beside it offers 5 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Crossover calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
